activities include field observations, key informant interviews and focus group sessions. The costs associated with undertaking the necessary monitoring,
assessments and engagements required to inform the project evaluations are presented in Annex 4: Detailed budget.
202. A project inception workshop will be held once the proposed project has been approved to: i) re-orient project stakeholders to the project strategy and discuss
any changes in the overall context that may influence project implementation; ii) discuss the roles and responsibilities of the project team, including reporting
and communication lines and conflict resolution mechanisms; iii) review the project Logical Framework; iv) discuss reporting, monitoring and evaluation roles
and responsibilities and finalise the M&E plan (Annex 11); v) review the financial reporting procedures and mandatory requirements, and agree on the
arrangements for the annual audit; and vi) plan and schedule Project Board meetings and finalise the first year annual work plan for the project. The final
inception report will be shared with the UNDP Country Office, UNDP Regional Technical Advisor and Project Board for clearance. Once the report has been
cleared by the relevant parties, it will be submitted to the GCF for approval. This will happen within six months after the Funded Activity Agreement (FAA)
becomes effective.
203. An annual progress report (APR) will be prepared by the Project Manager, UNDP Country Office, and UNDP Regional Technical Advisor for submission to
the GCF, Project Board and relevant project stakeholders. The Project Manager, supported by the Monitoring and Gender Officer, will ensure that the indicators
included in the project Logical Framework are monitored annually and that the results from regular M&E activities are presented in the GCF APR. Any challenges
and delays experienced during the implementation phase will be monitored by the Project Manager and reported in the GCF APR.
204. During the implementation phase, specific means of verification will be used to assess the: i) progress of project interventions towards achieving GCF Fund-
level impacts and Fund-level outcomes; and ii) performance of interventions against the project performance indicators presented in Section E.5 of this Funding
Proposal. A full-time Monitoring and Gender Officer will be employed to conduct and coordinate on-the-ground monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of the project
and ensure that gender targets are met. The Monitoring and Gender Officer will design and operationalise a performance monitoring framework to track the
project’s progress towards achieving its targets. This will be achieved by: i) measuring the performance against the project indicators (Sections E.3–5) to
evaluate the progress of the project; ii) reporting the project’s performance to the National Steering Committee (NSC) and Project Management Unit (PMU);
and iii) providing technical support to the Project Manager. Additionally, the Monitoring and Gender Officer will be responsible for overseeing and monitoring
the application of gender-disaggregated indicators140. At particular milestones (e.g. baseline, mid-term and project closure), the Monitoring and Gender Officer
will undertake evidence-gathering exercises to verify the project’s performance against the outcomes-based indicators presented in the Logical Framework,
M&E Plan and Gender Action Plan. The results from this process will be presented in periodic reports developed by the Monitoring and Gender Officer, supported
by the Project Manager. These reports will be submitted to the NSC and validated during the Independent Interim and Final Evaluations for the project, as
described below.
205. UNDP will be responsible for managing the Independent Interim (mid-term) and Final Evaluations of the project, including the process for contracting these
positions. For the Interim Evaluation, an independent consultant will be contracted to provide an assessment of project performance against its targets at the
project’s mid-term (end of Year 3). This will be an outcomes-based assessment and will include analysing whether the project is on track, what problems and
challenges the project is encountering, and what corrective actions are required, so that the project can achieve its intended outcomes by project completion in
the most efficient and sustainable way. Following this evaluation, the NSC will develop a management response to the evaluation recommendations along with
an implementation plan for undertaking the required actions. It is the responsibility of UNDP to assess whether the agreed recommendations are being
140 The project’s gender targets as well as the associated gender-disaggregated indicators are presented in Annex 8: Gender Assessment and Action Plan.

M&E records for this project for up to eight years after project financial closure to support ex-post evaluations.

RISK ASSESSMENT AND MANAGEMENT
F.1. Risk factors and mitigations measures (max. 3 pages)
Please describe financial, technical, operational, macroeconomic/political, money laundering/terrorist financing (ML/TF), sanctions,
prohibited practices, and other risks that might prevent the project/programme objectives from being achieved. Also describe the
proposed risk mitigation measures. Insert additional rows if necessary.
For probability: High has significant probability, Medium has moderate probability, Low has negligible probability
For impact: High has significant impact, Medium has moderate impact, Low has negligible impact
Prohibited practices include abuse, conflict of interest, corruption, retaliation against whistleblowers or witnesses, as well as
fraudulent, coercive, collusive, and obstructive practices
Selected Risk Factor 1
Category Probability Impact
Technical and operational Medium High
Description
Low survival rates of crops and trees planted during the project makes stabilisation of slopes ineffective, hampering
improvement in soil conservation measures.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Risk mitigation measures will include:
• Specifically selecting and using robust (ideally indigenous) species that are well adapted to local conditions, with
high levels of fire resistance and good re-sprouting capacity;
• Providing technical assistance to households implementing agroforestry;
• Involving the community in planning at the inception stage to foster ownership and promote long-term monitoring
and protection of planted sites;
• Practicing participatory planning for reforestation activities; and
• mobilising civil society to raise awareness of the importance of monitoring and protection of ground cover for
ecosystem service provision.
Selected Risk Factor 2
Category Probability Impact
Other Medium High
Description
Weak land-tenure, -use and -management systems prevent or delay implementation if agreements with landowners
or communities cannot be reached.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Ownership of project interventions will be supported by the development of Community Land Use Plans (under Activity
1.1), including assessing land-tenure and prioritising areas for interventions based on community recommendations
and agreements.
Since modifying the legislative framework for non-climate related aspects of land management is not within the scope
of the project, other risk mitigation measures include:
• ensuring the involvement and participation of target communities in the TR watershed at the inception and planning
stage to establish trust and support in the validation of land ownership;
• using the consultation process during the assessment phase as a platform to address concerns and increase buy-
in of communities;
• encouraging community involvement in IWRM at the sub-catchment level, helping to work towards more sustainable
agricultural and sub-catchment management practices; and
• capitalising upon top-down (e.g. establishment of the Water Act) and bottom-up (e.g. establishment and capacitating
of sub-catchment Water Resource Users’ Associations (WRUA)) approaches to land and water resources
management to ensure that local needs and experiences are considered during project implementation.

Selected Risk Factor 3
Category Probability Impact
Technical and operational Medium High
Description
Limited uptake of project interventions by target communities because of a preference towards fulfilling the
immediate need for sustenance through conventional agricultural techniques over long-term climate action.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Risk mitigation measures will include:
• building community interest by engaging Haitian civil society organisations (CSOs) and working with community
governance systems and associations to raise awareness of the challenges and impacts of climate change on
environmental degradation and food security;
• training and knowledge sharing initiatives to facilitate capacity building and ownership; and
• emphasising the introduction of more sustainable farming systems (i.e. agroforestry), sustainable (sub-)
catchment management and IWRM, as well as food security and nutrition interventions, which are designed to
be inclusive.
• Working with community members in monitoring the project’s indicators to establish a link between project action
and benefits.
Selected Risk Factor 4
Category Probability Impact
Governance Low Medium
Description
Inadequate national focus on adaptation measures because of other development pressures affecting the
sustainability of the proposed project beyond GCF involvement.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Risk mitigation will consider:
• building resilience into watershed management is increasingly becoming a national priority and is expected to
develop into a sustained focus on adaptation in Haiti; and
• a participatory and inclusive processes to help institutionalise climate change adaptation and ensure the
sustainability of the integrated management approach.
• Embedding the project within national policy efforts including water management and the National Adaptation
Plan process
Selected Risk Factor 5
Category Probability Impact
Other Medium High
Description
Continued overexploitation and unregulated land-use and -tenure renders soil conservation measures redundant,
causing increasing degradation and permanent losses in soil fertility.
Mitigation Measure(s)
• Through an integrated flood management planning approach, the project is intended to address environmental
degradation partially and indirectly by framing regulations pertaining to land-use in areas directly impacted by
climate change.
• Additionally, improved institutional capacity will also contribute to reducing degradative practices through better
planning, policy decision-making and natural resource-management capacities.
• The risk will further be mitigated by shifting practices and garnering buy-in of the local community through
consultations to promote active involvement in sub-catchment IWRM, participation in crop/tree planting activities
and building awareness of climate change impacts by mobilising the CSOs.

planning, policy decision-making and natural resource-management capacities.
• The risk will further be mitigated by shifting practices and garnering buy-in of the local community through
consultations to promote active involvement in sub-catchment IWRM, participation in crop/tree planting activities
and building awareness of climate change impacts by mobilising the CSOs. |  |

Category Probability Impact
Governance Low Low
Description
Weak coordination between stakeholders, climate initiatives and implementation partners reduce the effectiveness
of IWRM approaches in Haiti.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The risk will be mitigated by promoting coordination through the strategic identification of established multi-
stakeholder groups, including the WRUAs at sub-catchment level and the CIWRMC at catchment level.
Coordination between these groups will be strengthened through workshops and knowledge-sharing initiatives
aimed at: i) building awareness of activities being undertaken; ii) developing best practices to draw from; iii)
synchronising efforts; and iv) replicating successes from each project.
Risk will further be reduced by involving multiple actors in supporting catchment IWRM, including NGOs, private
development organisations and community-based organisations. The participation of these entities will complement
the relevant stakeholders within MoE and other relevant sector ministries, contributing towards coordination and
integration of interests, needs and perspectives.
The project will report regularly to the Technical Secretariat of the National Committee on Climate Change to ensure
alignment with the GoH own Climate Strategies including the country’s National Adapation Plan. The project will
also shares result with development partners and agencies through the the various donor groups for the
environmental sector and for disaster risk reduction.

Category Probability Impact
Other Medium High
Description

Mitigation Measure(s)
Mitigation measures include:
• land-use plans taking these risks into account;
• accelerating project execution during non-peak wet weather periods; and
• choosing tree varieties and timing of planting to favour fast-growing species during the first planting cycle to
shield crops and newly planted seedlings from extreme weather events.

Selected Risk Factor 9
Category Probability Impact
Other Medium Medium
Description
Insecurity within the country may seep into project sites particularly in Bassin Bleu and Gros Morne and cause
delays in the implementation of project activities.
Mitigation Measure(s)
An initial conflict analyis has been prepared by the project and included within the project’s ESMF. The analysis
and the project’s ESFM provideds guidelines for the development of Security Plans and Conflict Assessments that
will be developed as part of the activity level EISAs/ESMFs during the project’s first year and will result in activity
specific management plans per grouped areas. To reduce the potential of project beneficiaries or staff being
targeted by illegal actors, the project has avoided the provision of direct cash benefits focusing more on community
based benefits (capacity building, agroforestry inputs, enhanced associative capacity, etc.). In terms of mobility,
UNDSS rules will be used and strictly adhered to by the project particularly during internal travel and security issues
will be continuously monitored to allow for adaptive management in case it is required. Procurement strategies will
favor local purchases to avoid any potential danger in the transport of project equipment and its delivery to project
sites. In addittion, a logistics and operations officer has been foreseen by the project to ensure that logistics take
into account insecurity risks when planning the delivery of project activities and on the ground missions.The
project’s community based approach will allow for the project to ensure strong community buy in and enhance
social capital, this approach will help develop community informed practices in the implementation of project
activities to avoid potential security risks while creating an opportunity to maximise the peacebuilding potential of
the project.

GCF POLICIES AND STANDARDS
G.1. Environmental and social risk assessment (max. 750 words, approximately 1.5 pages)
208. This project has completed the UNDP social and environmental screening procedure undertaken to ensure it
complies with UNDP’s Social and Environmental Standards. The social and environmental risk category for this
project is: Moderate (Category B). A detailed risk assessment undertaken for the project Social and Environmental
Risk Procedure (SESP), as well as the Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF), are presented
in Annex 6.
209. UNDP will be responsible for the ESMF, ensuring it is adequate and followed. The PMU will be responsible for
the revision or updates of the ESMF document during project implementation and will ensure timely corrective
actions are taken, as identified. Any non-conformances to the ESMF are to be noted in environmental inspections
and logged into the register. Depending on the severity of the non- conformance, the Site Supervisor may specify
a corrective action on the site inspection report. The ESMF and its procedures are to be reviewed at least every
year by UNDP staff and the MoE. The objective of the review is to update the document to reflect knowledge gained
during project delivery/construction and to reflect new knowledge and changed community standards (values).
210. The progress of all corrective actions will be tracked using the register. Any non-conformances and the issue of
corrective actions are to be advised to UNDP. UNDP and the MoE will also release updates on the project on a
regular basis to provide interested stakeholders with information on project status. Updates may be via a range of
media, for example print, radio, social media or formal reports, and all material must be published in English and
Haitian Creole (Kreyòl) as appropriate. A publicised telephone number will be maintained throughout the project to
serve as a point of contact for enquiries, concerns, complaints and/or grievances. All enquiries, concerns,
complaints and/or grievances will be recorded on a register and the appropriate manager will be informed.
211. The project has the potential to cause low to moderate environmental and social impacts. The Project’s design
has avoided all high-risk environmental and social impacts and favoured a wholly climate resilient infrastructure
approach to flood management, eschewing high-risk grey infrastructure for flood control. Furthermore, the project
does not require any land acquisition and/or resettlement, does not promote the use of pesticides and fertilisers,
prohibits the use of alien invasive species in planting, and promotes diverse agroforestry systems and reforestation
that will not only build climate resilience and food security, and decrease the impact of floods, but also provide
significant environmental and social co-benefits.
212. When undertaking the risk assessment, all activities were assessed, with an emphasis on those with the potential
for some adverse risk, specifically Output 1, Activity 1.2 which involves the project’s physical interventions
(agroforestry and reforestation) financed by GCF. Potential risks identified include: i) the possibility that activities
reproduce discriminations against women based on gender, due to existing structural inequalities and roles in
agriculture and decision-making; ii) the possibility that activities lead to the unintentional increased use of pesticides
and fertilisers in agroforestry systems because of improved income; and iii) a low risk that there is a possibility of
child labour use in the promoted agroforestry systems. Specific measures for each environmental and social risk
are discussed along with mitigation measures in the ESMF.
213. The preparation of the ESMF included public consultation as part of the Stakeholder Engagement Plan. The full
Stakeholder Engagement Plan is appended as part of the proposal in Annex 7: Stakeholder Engagement Plan,
which includes the full list of stakeholders consulted, and a summary of the consultations. The project was
discussed with a wide range of stakeholders including relevant government departments, industry groups, NGOs,
and individual community members (including marginalised groups) and was approved by the Government of Haiti.
These extensive on-the-ground consultations undertaken during the design of the project (as well as during the
earlier interventions that this project complements and up-scales) closely informed overall project design and the
ESMF, and it is expected that consultations with affected communities and beneficiaries will continue. It is
anticipated that based on the communities’ needs, the projects will be fully accepted.

214. A Gender Assessment and Action Plan (GAAP) was developed for this project in order to provide an overview of
the issue of gender in Haiti, with a specific focus on the gender differentiated impacts of climate change and how
this information can be used to design a gender-sensitive adaptation intervention. The GAAP identifies gender
issues relevant to the project interventions and situated in the Haitian context, across elements such as use and
access to resources, gender-differentiated roles in employment and livelihoods, and roles in political decision

G.2. Gender assessment and action plan (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
214. A Gender Assessment and Action Plan (GAAP) was developed for this project in order to provide an overview of
the issue of gender in Haiti, with a specific focus on the gender differentiated impacts of climate change and how
this information can be used to design a gender-sensitive adaptation intervention. The GAAP identifies gender
issues relevant to the project interventions and situated in the Haitian context, across elements such as use and
access to resources, gender-differentiated roles in employment and livelihoods, and roles in political decision

=== PAGE 104 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 100
F
making. The Gender Action Plan specifically describes opportunities for gender mainstreaming in the project design
so that the proposed project interventions address gendered climate resilience across the household, community
and institutional levels.
215. Haiti ranks third globally on the Long-Term Climate Risk Index142, demonstrating its extreme vulnerability to
climate change — to which women are especially vulnerable. Widespread deforestation and soil degradation have
so severely impacted the island’s environment that it can no longer provide critical ecosystem functions, such as
mitigating the effects of heavy rain and flooding. This has progressively increased human vulnerability to climate
change. Extreme climate events, such as tropical storms and hurricanes, are expected to increase in frequency
and intensity, while rainfall is expected to become more erratic across seasons143. In an already denuded and
degraded landscape, this increased rainfall engenders severe erosion and landslides, flash flooding, and
sedimentation of river channels144.
216. Climate change impacts are not gender-neutral and many of the consequences of climate-induced impacts are
more severe for women, and other socio-economically marginalised groups, given their specific livelihood
circumstances. In relative terms, women lack access to productive resources, and this has impacts on their health,
food security and safety in the context of flooding and other extreme climate events. The additional socio-cultural
barriers limiting participation and movement outside the household sphere is worsened by phenomena such as
flooding, drought and erratic rainfall. These constraints cause women to have to work much harder to secure food
and water, and generate additional income through livelihoods which, in turn, diminishes their ability to advance
out of poverty, particularly when they have, for example, lost their land due to the impacts of flooding during cyclone
events.
217. Gender equality and women’s empowerment are not addressed in most of Haiti’s strategy or action plan
documents for climate change and disaster risk management145, 146. Flooding has cumulative livelihood effects that
unfairly impact women and exacerbate gender inequality. In Haiti, women are disproportionately represented
among the poor and there is a significant portion of women-headed households, so impacts such as crop loss,
animal drowning, destroyed homes, health risks or displacement and loss of life resulting from floods ultimately
affect women to a higher extent. Yet, during these extreme flooding events, the importance of grassroots
organisation and mobilisation of women’s groups during disaster relief efforts has been unparalleled and critical,
demonstrating the resilience of Haitian women in the face of extreme adversity.
218. Over 40% of households in Haiti are headed by women, and this percentage has been on the rise since 2007147,
148. Today, there are more women living under extreme poverty than men, with a large proportion residing in rural
areas149. Most of Haiti’s population is rural, and two-thirds of this population is dependent on agriculture; with
women comprising a significant portion of the labour force involved across all aspects of agricultural processes150.
219. To address gender dimensions within the project design and implementation, the Gender Action Plan will account
for:
• specific strategies to include/target female-headed households;
• differing conservation incentives faced by women;
• identification of gaps in gender equality through the use of sex-disaggregated data enabling the gender action
plan to close those gaps, devoting resources and expertise for implementing such strategies, monitoring the
results of implementation, and holding individuals and institutions accountable for outputs that promote gender
equality;
• advocacy and awareness that is adjusted to most effectively reflect gender-specific differences; and
• the inclusion of a Gender Specialist position/provision of advice within the project to implement gender-related
activities.

220. Gender benefits through this project have been optimised by promoting the full involvement of women in decision-
making regarding integrated flood management at the community and institutional levels, as well as promoting
women as the stewards of agroforestry systems, playing key roles in the selection of species and transformation
of products. In addition, as during the design of the project, strong efforts will continue to be made during
implementation to ensure the equitable participation of women. Additionally, going forward beyond the
implementation phase, equal participation of women will be pursued and achieved in ongoing management and
water governance especially on the Water Governance Committees.
221. During project implementation, qualitative assessments will be conducted on the gender-specific benefits that
can be directly attributed to the project. This will be incorporated in the annual Project Implementation Report, Mid-
Term Report, and Terminal Evaluation. Indicators to quantify the achievement of project objectives in relation to
gender equality will include men and women who had access to affordable solutions, number of men and women
employed from the jobs created by the project, training opportunities, knowledge management and information
dissemination.
222. The stakeholder consultations and engagement of women’s organisations promote gender equality at the local
as well as the national level. The involvement of women’s organisations in the project design aided in identifying
relevant gender issues within the country’s social context, as well as in implementing and monitoring the gender
aspects of the project.
G.3. Financial management and procurement (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
223. The financial management and procurement of this project will be guided by UNDP financial rules and regulations
available here151. Further guidance is outlined in the financial resources management section of the UNDP Program
and Operations Policies and Procedures (POPP) available here. UNDP has comprehensive procurement policies
in place as outlined in the ‘Contracts and Procurement’ section of UNDP’s POPP. See here.
224. The project will be implemented following the full-support National Implementation Modality (NIM) following the
UNDP’s POPP guidelines available here152. UNDP will ascertain the national capacities of the implementing partner
by undertaking an evaluation of capacity following the Framework for Cash Transfers to Implementing Partners
(part of the Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfers - Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfer (HACT). All projects
will be audited following the UNDP financial rules and regulations noted above and applicable audit guidelines and
policies.
225. The Full Support to NIM guidelines are a formal part of UNDP’s policies and procedures, as set out in the
UNDP POPP. The NIM guidelines were corporately developed and adopted by UNDP and are fully compliant with
UNDP’s procurement and financial management rules and regulations.
226. The national executing entity MoE (also referred to as the national ‘Implementing Partner’ in UNDP terminology),
is required to implement the project in compliance with UNDP rules and regulations, policies, and procedures
(including the NIM guidelines). In legal terms, this is ensured through the national Government’s signature of the
UNDP Standard Basic Assistance Agreement (SBAA), together with a UNDP project document which will be signed
by the Implementing Partner to govern the use of the funds. Both of these documents require compliance. During
implementation, UNDP will provide oversight and quality assurance in accordance with its policies and procedures,
and any specific requirements in the Accreditation Master Agreement (AMA) and project confirmation to be agreed
with the GCF. This may include, but is not limited to, monitoring missions, spot checks, facilitation and participation
in project board meetings, quarterly progress and annual implementation reviews, and audits at project level or at
implementing partner level on the resources received from UNDP.
151 In line with UNDP National Implementation (NIM) Guidelines, the Government is responsible for the management and procurement of the
Project to achieve project outputs. Government regulations, rules and procedures apply to project implementation to the extent that they do
not contravene the principles of the Financial Regulations and Rules of UNDP. UNDP Financial Regulations section 16.05 state:
- “The administration by executing entities or, under the harmonized operational modalities, implementing partners, of resources obtained
from or through UNDP shall be carried out under their respective financial regulations, rules, practices and procedures only to the extent
that they do not contravene the principles of the Financial Regulations and Rules of UNDP.
- Where the financial governance of an executing entity or, under the harmonized operational modalities, implementing partner, does not
provide the required guidance to ensure best value for money, fairness, integrity, transparency, and effective international competition that
of UNDP shall apply.”

F
The project will be audited in accordance with UNDP policies and procedures on audits, informed by and together
with any specific requirements agreed in the AMA. According to the current audit policies, UNDP will be appointing
the auditors. In UNDP, scheduled audits are performed during the project cycle as per UNDP assurance/audit plans,
based on the implementing partner's risk rating and UNDP’s guidelines. A scheduled audit is used to determine
whether the funds transferred to the implementing partner were used for the appropriate purpose and in accordance
with the work plan. A scheduled audit can consist of a financial audit and/or an internal control audit.
G.4. Disclosure of funding proposal
Note: The Information Disclosure Policy (IDP) provides that the GCF will apply a presumption in favour of disclosure
for all information and documents relating to the GCF and its funding activities. Under the IDP, project and
programme funding proposals will be disclosed on the GCF website, simultaneous with the submission to the Board,
subject to the redaction of any information that may not be disclosed pursuant to the IDP. Information provided in
confidence is one of the exceptions, but this exception should not be applied broadly to an entire document if the
document contains specific, segregable portions that can be disclosed without prejudice or harm.
Indicate below whether or not the funding proposal includes confidential information.
☒ No confidential information: The accredited entity confirms that the funding proposal, including its annexes, may
be disclosed in full by the GCF, as no information is being provided in confidence.
☐ With confidential information: The accredited entity declares that the funding proposal, including its annexes, may
not be disclosed in full by the GCF, as certain information is being provided in confidence. Accordingly, the accredited
entity is providing to the Secretariat the following two copies of the funding proposal, including all annexes:
• full copy for internal use of the GCF in which the confidential portions are marked accordingly, together with
an explanatory note regarding the said portions and the corresponding reason for confidentiality under the
accredited entity’s disclosure policy, and
• redacted copy for disclosure on the GCF website.
The funding proposal can only be processed upon receipt of the two copies above, if containing confidential
information.

=== PAGE 115 ===

Page 115
3.
Haiti is a small island developing State (SIDS) and the only least developed country
(LDC) in the Caribbean region. The geographical location, heavy dependence on climate-
sensitive livelihoods, and high level of longstanding macroeconomic challenges make Haiti
highly vulnerable to hydrometeorological disasters. In particular, projected climate change
impacts including temperature rise, greater annual rainfall variability, and more frequent and
intense hurricanes will lead to increased and more severe flooding events. Between 1975 and
2012, floods, tropical storms and hurricanes resulted in economic damage and losses equivalent
to 2 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product on average per year. As such, the
Governm ent of Haiti has prioritized watershed management actions in its national adaptation
plan in the Northwest and the Aribonite regions where the Trois-Rivières (TR) watershed is
lo cated.
4.
Although the TR watershed is not the largest watershed in the country, its population is
particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change-induced flooding, with limited
resources to adequately adapt or respond to such events. The rural areas of the TR catchment
have an extreme poverty rate of 40 per cent, which is almost twice the national average of 23.9
per cent and much higher than any other area of Haiti. This project will provide a suite of
interventions to enhance the resilience of the population and ecosystems of the TR region and
pr omote a transformative approach to the flood management system in the TR watershed.
5.
The objective of this project is to enhance the climate resilience of the TR region by
initiating a shift away from uncoordinated decision-making and unsustainable land -use
practices towards an integrated, climate-resilient approach to land and water resources
ma nagement. This will be achieved through the following integrated components:
(a)
Ecosystem-based flood management solutions implemented in 25,440 ha of the TR
watershed;
(b)
Climate-resilient agricu ltural practices, optimized value chains and social safety nets
established to promote sustainable landscape management and reduce degradation in
the TR watershed; and
(c)
Strengthened governance and capacity for climate-resilient integrated water resources
management (IWRM).
6.
The project will directly benefit at least 292,600 people, of which 52 per cent are
women, in the seven target communes across the TR region of Haiti, which accounts for about 3
per cent of the country’s total population. These are the most vulnerable populations of Haiti
who have limited adaptive capacity to cope with the increased frequency of flooding and will
benefit from the project’s combination of int erventions detailed below. The project will also
indirectly benefit an additional 441,272 people, of which 52 per cent are women (approximately
4 per cent of the entire population of Haiti).
7.
The total project financing is USD 31,290,561, with a request for GCF grants of USD
22,427,206. Heifer International Haiti will provide co-finance of USD 8,303,355 in the form of
grants, and United National Development Programme (UNDP) will also provide grant co-
financing of USD 560,000. The project is submitted under environmental and social safeguards
(ESS) category B.
2Co.2mponCenotm 1:p Eoconseysntetm-b-bya-sceodm flopood nmeannat gaenmaelnyt ssoislu tions implemented in 25,440 hectares of
the Trois-Rivières watershed (total cost: USD 18.40 million; GCF cost: USD 18.20 million)
8.
Component 1 aims to directly enhance the resilience of the TR catchment by
implementing agroforestry systems and restoration of arboreal land cover on degraded
mountainous slopes in the TR watershed. An increase in concentrated and heavy rainfall,

=== PAGE 116 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.03
Page 116
combined with the increasing frequency and intensity of hurricanes and tropical storms, has
resulted in the rapid erosion of fertile soils throughout the TR watershed. This is exacerbated by
the steep topography and highly deforested landscape of the watershed, which intensifies flow
rates because of reduced ground cover and further increases erosion and river sedimentation.
The combination of these factors often results in the destruction of crops, farmlands and
agricultural infrastructure, as well as a loss of livestock and human lives during the flood events.
The implementation of the proposed ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA) flood management
solutions is expected to address these issues by significantly reducing peak run-off and flooding
extent in the area by increasing vegetative cover in the watershed and the infiltration capacity
of the soil. More specifically, the agroforestry systems will be implemented in 17,740 ha of
degraded land, and reforestation and restoration will be implemented in 7,700 ha of forest
ar eas across the target areas.
9.
The proposed activities include establishing nurseries, planting seedlings (e.g. for fruit
production and reforestation) and providing ongoing technical assistance to end users including
on establishing and monitoring of nurseries, scheduling seedling planting, using technical
packages for agroforestry and monitoring the agroforestry systems to account for the growing
times of many agroforestry species. The spaces between the agroforestry species will be filled
with perennial food crops (e.g. plantains, sugar cane, cassava, pigeon peas and pineapple), in
co mbination with annual crops (e.g. sweet potato, yams and other annuals).
10.
This intervention, which is an example of EbA, will be supplemented by developing the
capacity of the target community groups, including farmers’ and women’s associations
regarding climate-resilient land-use planning. Thirty-three communities within the seven target
communes in the TR watershed will receive this training, which will then result in the
development of 33 community land-use plans, through community engagement in a
consultative process. These plans will focus on identifying the impacts of climate change,
particularly flooding, on the TR watershed and designing appropriate actions for addressing
these impacts. Such actions include the implementation of EbA solutions to reduce flood risk in
the watershed as well as the promotion of sustainable, climate-resilient land-use practices and
techniques to reduce the risk of increased land degradation under future climate change
conditions. The farmers in the target areas will receive training on developing sustainable
agroforestry business models that will contribute to both improving livelihood security and
enhancing the use of sustainable land-use practices. This participatory approach will ensure
Component 2: Climate-resilient agricultural practices, optimized value chains and social safety
that the proposed interventions will have buy-in from beneficiary groups.
nets established to promote sustainable landscape management and reduce degradation in the
Trois-Rivières watershed (total cost: USD 8.30 million; GCF cost: USD 0)
11.
Component 2 will facilitate a transformative shift in Haiti’s agricultural sector from
unsustainable practices (e.g. the cultivation of annual crop types and clearing of forests for
charcoal production) towards sustainable options that are resilient to the impacts of climate
change-induced flooding. This shift will result in sustainable livelihoods for the populations of
the TR region, while reducing deforestation and land degradation and maintaining the integrity
of its land and soil. In turn, this will contribute to decreasing flood damage, and a virtuous cycle
will be created in the integrated flood management practices in this region. This component will
be entirely funded and implemented by Heifer International for this project with its co-finance
funding. A suite of complementary activities will be implemented to achieve this component
including: (1) strengthening the institutional capacity of the people who are involved in the
technical aspects of agriculture at the target commune, inter-commune and department levels
for implementing sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural practices; (2) enhancing access
to financial resources for smallholder farmers in order to facilitate the uptake and
implementation of climate-resilient agricultural practices over the long term; and (3)
establishing a social protection system for households that face chronic food insecurity. The co-

=== PAGE 117 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.03
Page 117
finance funding for this component will be catalysed by the approval of the GCF amount, and the
Component 3: Strengthened governance and capacity for climate-resilient integrated water
sequence of activities will be aligned in order to maximize the impacts of these activities.
resources management (total cost: USD 3.27 million; GCF cost: USD 3.27 million)
12.
Component 3 will strengthen the capacity of the Government of Haiti to develop and
implement the Water Act, which will be an indispensable legal foundation for enabling
participatory IWRM in the TR watershed. The current water governance system in Haiti is
organized at both the departmental and the communal level, which creates an overlap between
different bodies, particularly at the catchment and sub-catchment levels. This poses challenges
in coordination and planning among stakeholders at different levels and leads to ineffective and
inefficient implementation of an integrated approach to water resources management in the TR
watershed. The activities envisaged under this component include: (1) drafting provisions to
Haiti’s Water Act for the adoption of an integrated approach to water resources management;
(2) establishing catchment IWRM committees within 31 catchments in Haiti; and (3)
establishing sub-catchment water resource users’ associations within the sub-catchments of the
31 catchments. These committees will work with different stakeholders in the 31 catchments
and sub-catchments to manage the efficient use of land and water resources and will be
responsible for fostering community empowerment and ownership over these critical resources
under future climate change conditions. These activities will ensure that the Water Act is
developed and implemented to respond not only to national level priorities, but also to the
Project management (total cost: USD 1.31 million; GCF cost: USD 0.95 million)
adaptation needs of vulnerable communities living in the TR watershed.
13.
The GCF portion of this project management cost is less than 5 per cent of the total
requested GCF funding and is compliant with the GCF policy on fees.
III. Assessment of performance against investment criteria
Scale: N/A
3.1 Impact potential
14.
The proposed project will directly benefit 292,600 people (2.7 per cent of the total
population), targeting the most vulnerable population.
15.
The project net present value (NPV) of interventions is estimated to be USD 207 million
with an internal rate of return (IRR) of 37.9 per cent, and therefore represents a highly cost-
effective spend for the Government of Haiti. The estimated health benefits under the economic
and financial analysis list water-borne diseases (such as diarrhoea and cholera) that would,
without the project interventions, likely increase in prevalence because of increased flooding
and related impacts.
16.
The increase in tree cover (17,740 ha agroforestry and 7,700 ha restoration) is
expected to result in a 40 per cent reduction in peak run-off and reduce floodplain extents by 26
1
per cent in the areas with a 1 per cent annual exceedance probability (AEP) of floods.
Scale: N/A
3.2 Paradigm shift potential
17.
The proposed project will catalyse a paradigm shift in Haiti’s approach to flood
management in the TR watershed by initiating a shift away from uncoordinated decision-

making and unsustainable land-use practices towards an integrated, climate-resilient approach

18.
Firstly, agroforestry systems will be established and degraded forests restored at

3. 3 Sustainable development potential
19.
Under the project, the technical and institutional capacity of relevant stakeholders at the
national, department and commune levels will be strengthened regarding implementation of an
integrated approach to land and water resources management that is centred around
sustainability and climate resilience. By building the capacity of the targeted institutions, the
transfer of knowledge and skills related to sustainable watershed and flood management will
ex tend beyond the project.
20.
Strengthening the Water Act will establish a legal foundation for optimizing the use of
water resources without compromising the sustainability of vital ecosystems under future
climate change conditions, consequently securing equitable economic and social welfare. The
Water Act will also provide a framework for the institutionalization of integrated watershed
management to empower regional administrations across Haiti – through establishing
catchment water resources management committees and sub-catchment water resource users
ass ociations.
21.
This country-driven project has been developed using a participatory and consultative
process, enabling all relevant stakeholders to contribute to the design of interventions, ensuring
buy-in and commitment from national- and local-level stakeholders. More importantly to
communities, the social protection system provided through the project. as well as the EbA
interventions that will be installed, will provide tangible benefits to communities linking the
IWRM approach to reduced vulnerability.
Scale: N/A
3. 4 Needs of the recipient
22.
Haiti is a SIDS and an LDC hit by cascading and compounding climate hazards (floods,
hurricanes, tropical storms, erosions, etc). The target beneficiaries endure double the national
average poverty rate. The watershed is particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change-
induced flooding. Given the near-complete absence of embankments and levees in the
watershed, such flooding causes severe damage to crops and farmland, as well as agricultural
infrastructure and equipment. Flooding in the region also has severe consequences for both
human and livestock health, resulting in an increased risk of loss of human life and livestock.
Addressing the impact of climate change-induced flooding on vulnerable communities in the
region requires the adoption of an integrated approach to flood management that responds to
the impacts of climate change.
23.
At present, the Government of Haiti does not have the capacity to fully finance
integrated climate-resilient flood management interventions through domestic finance in both

=== PAGE 119 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.03
Page 119
the private and public sector. Without GCF support, the Government of Haiti will continue to
operate under the existing paradigm of reactive recovery from the impacts of climate change.
Scale: N/A
3. 5 Country ownership
24.
The project is a direct contribution to Haiti’s adaptation targets in relation to watershed
management, coastal and marine protection, and reforestation, as reflected in the updated
nationally determined contribution submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on
Climate Change in 2022 and responds to the institutional capacity needs identified in Haiti’s
national adaptation plan submitted in early 2023. The project is also a prioritized intervention
with GCF and is included in the advanced draft country programme which, at the time of
writing, was in the last stages of preparation. In this regard the no-objection letter was issued
an d cleared in April 2022.
25.
Extensive stakeholder consultations were held during the project elaboration and
feedback was incorporated into the development of the proposal. Active stakeholder
engagement, notably in the intervention areas, is planned to ensure optimal execution of the
project and as part of the adaptive management strategy of the project.
Scale: N/A
3. 6 Efficiency and effectiveness
26.
The funding proposal package presents economic and financial analyses with reasonable
assumptions as well as a clear definition of scope and the counterfactual scenarios. The
economic analysis contains estimations of all the relevant economic values from the project
activities that are consistent with the information provided in the funding proposal. The model
uses a social discount rate of 10 per cent in line with all the other UNDP projects. In summary,
the economic model results show the NPV ranging between USD 375 million and USD 412
million with an IRR of 41 per cent and 43 per cent depending on the different flood reduction
sce narios. The model shows that the proposed project is economically viable.
27.
The financial analysis has been conducted at the individual farmer’s perspective for the
agroforestry activity, assessing whether the farmers would be able to invest in the agroforestry
activities described in the funding proposal through their own resources or other existing
sources of finance (microfinance, bank loans, etc.) The weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
used is 3.7 per cent as the mean of the lowest and highest nominal monthly rates charged by
microfinance institutions in peer group and village banks. The financial IRR is above the WACC,
although grants are still requested, on the basis of the sensitivity analysis conducted with loan
sce narios.
28.
Financial adequacy and appropriate of concessionality is assessed to be high. The
accredited entity (AE) has conducted a sensitivity analysis for the agroforestry model and
calculated financial profitability indicators for the agroforestry model (NPV, financial IRR and
payback period) in four cases: (1) when activities are fully financed by farmers on their own
(“without project”); (2) when activities are financed with GCF grants (“with project”); (3) when
activities are financed with bank loans at the lowest interest rates (2.75 per cent); and (4) when
activities are financed with bank loans at the highest interest rates (4.8 per cent). The results
show that the agroforestry activities cannot be financed with full bank loans (negative cash
flows), and the payback period would be too long for low interest rate loans. An analysis of the
mi x of loans and grants scenario has not been conducted.
29.
The need for grants in this project is also justified by the public nature of the project
activities. The funding proposal describes the absence of financing for the proposed activities
for farmers as one of the major barriers. Alternative sources of funding and credit are not
available or are difficult to access, leading farmers to go for the option of short-term relief

=== PAGE 120 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.03
Page 120
activities, such as the production of charcoal at unsustainable rates to meet pressing short-term
fin ancial needs.
30.
The project’s adaptation cost is USD 78/direct beneficiary and USD 31/total beneficiary.
Cost per direct beneficiary is in line with the portfolio average for Latin America and the
Caribbean. The co-financing ratio is 1:0.39, which is lower than the target set in the updated
Strategic Plan for the GCF 2020–2023. The proposal does not present a clear roadmap or
prospect about the potential for leveraging or mobilizing additional financial resources.

and planning mechanisms to be developed in seven communes targeted by the project in the TR
watershed, namely Port-de-Paix, Chansolme, Bassin Bleu, Plaisance, Pilate, Marmelade, and Gros
Morne. The project will improve climate resilience and food security, decrease the impact of
floods, and provide significant environmental and social co-benefits, through ecosystem-based

The AE has triggered its own standard on

to support their economic well-being. To be developed as part of the ESMP, the LAP will address
beneficiary participation in economic displacement decision-making, adequate (full and fair)

are improved. The LAP will include independent monitoring procedures, clarification of land

41.
As listed in the project’s exclusionary criteria, the project will exclude project
activities that will be implemented in areas of critical habitats, unless all of the following are
demonstrated. That is, (i) there are no measurable adverse impacts on the criteria or
biodiversity values for which the critical habitat was designated, and on the ecological processes
supporting those biodiversity values (determined on an ecologically-relevant scale); (ii) there is
no reduction of any recognized Endangered, Vulnerable or Critically Endangered species, (iii)
any lesser impacts are mitigated, and (iv) a robust, appropriately designed, and long-term
Biodiversity Action Plan is in place to achieve net gains of those biodiversity values for which
the critical habitat was designated. The project will exclude activities that involve the
application of chemical fertilizers or pesticides as a result of the agroforestry and reforestation
interventions of the project, as well as activities that risk the introduction of alien and
potentially invasive alien species. Despite such exclusion, the ESMF identifies that the project
could expose substantial risks on biodiversity due to that Port-de-Paix, one of the targeted
project sites, is a KBA and an Alliance for Zero Extinction (AZE) site. This KBA falls within the
project’s AREA 2 encompassing the semiarid areas across Gros-morne, Chansolme, Port-de-Paix,
and Bassin Bleu. The AE expects that the community land use plan for this area (under Sub
activity 1.1.1) may be developed potentially within or adjacent to this KBA. The ESMF requires
that the decision as to whether project activities will take place within or adjacent to this KBA
and other critical habitats must follow the mitigation hierarchy as described in the ESMF. If
project activities take place within or adjacent to a KBA, those activities must be guided by an
appropriately scoped and detailed Biodiversity Action Plan (BAP) to create positive impacts on
biodiversity conservation and in line with the requirements of AE’s relevant and guidance. The
project will assess its potential impacts on biodiversity and natural resources more clearly at
the start of the project implementation, through conducting a SESA and site-specific ESIAs.
Depending on the scope of the project activities to be designed at the site-level, mitigation
measures will be formulated as part of the site-specific ESMP or as a standalone Biodiversity
Management Plan (BMP). The ESMF provides detailed guidance for the development of context
specific BAP or BMP to ensure that the project will achieve net gains to the biodiversity values

Grievance redress mechanism (GRM).
47.
The ESMF provides the principles for the
development of a project-level GRM and a compliant register, which will handle community-
related issues during construction works. Any complaint and/or grievance will be advised to the
AE and EE within 24 hours of receipt. The ESMF requires a summary list of complaints and/or
grievances received, and their disposition to be published in a report produced every six
months. The project-level GRM will be operationalized at the start of the project implementation
to address all complaints and/or grievances in the project. The stakeholders will be informed of
the various means for making complaints and/or grievances, including in addition to the
project-level and national grievance redress mechanisms, the option to access AE’s own
accountability mechanism that has both the compliance and grievance functions. A social and
environmental compliance unit hosted by the AE’s office of audit and investigations will
investigate allegations regarding the AE's standards, screening procedure, or other E&S
commitments that are not being implemented adequately, and that harm may result to people
or the environment. A compliance review is available to any community or individual with
concerns about the impacts of the AE’s programmes or projects. The unit is mandated by the AE
to independently and impartially investigate valid requests from locally impacted people, and to
report its findings and recommendations publicly. The ESMF also include the GCF’s Independent
Redress Mechanism as an integral of the project’s GRM.
4. 2 Gender policy
48.
The AE provided a gender assessment and action plan with the funding proposal and
therefore complies with the requirements of the GCF Gender Policy. The assessment was
informed by secondary data and outcomes from the consultations during mission visits by the
pr oject development team.
49.
The climate change and disaster risk management legislative frameworks in Haiti do not
adequately address the issues of gender equality and the empowerment of women. However,
flooding and other natural disasters have cumulative livelihood effects that unfairly impact
women and exacerbate gender inequality. Evidence and impacts were drawn from the 2010
earthquake and 2015 Hurricane Matthew. In Haiti, women are disproportionately represented
among the poor and there is a significant proportion of women-headed households, so impacts
such as crop loss, livestock drowning, destroyed homes or displacement, and health risks and
loss of life due to floods ultimately affect women first and foremost. Gender-based violence is
another issue that normally goes unnoticed and unreported, including police violence targeting
women and marginalized groups. Of the cases of violence reported between 2009 and 2011, the
majority were physical in nature (59.74 per cent), followed by sexual violence (29.80 per cent),
while cases of psychological and economic violence constituted a minority (5.88 per cent and
4.5 8 per cent, respectively).
50.
From this gender assessment, various gender-responsive approaches have been
proposed, including building a strong collaboration with public water resources departments in
ensuring that the design and installation of water infrastructure facilities are based on gender
assessments; increasing the capacity of local government on women’s leadership and
participation in water management; supporting local municipal authorities and communities to
develop and maintain gender-equitable distribution of water resources; and ensuring that
partnerships with the private sector include a commitment to gender equality and that women
receive equal access to technical or management training, peer-to-peer learning and other
resources. Other gender recommendations have been made in the areas of agricultural and
climate change resilience, reforestation and agroforestry systems, including promoting land
ownership and other productive resources in forest management and climate mitigation
strategies.

=== PAGE 126 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.03
Page 126
51.
A gender and safeguards expert (at programme management unit level) will be
responsible for the implementation of the gender action plan (GAP) in collaboration with Heifer
International (the EE for outcome 2). Gender technical expertise and assistance will also be
sought on an ad hoc basis to supplement the available skill set and experience within the
programme management unit. The expected outcome of the GAP is improved capacities for an
estimated 87,780–146,300 women (30–50 per cent of project direct beneficiaries) on
sustainable water and land management as a means to enhance their resilience to climate
change. Some of the activities outlined in the GAP include (1) strengthening the capacity of
community groups, farmer and women’s associations in climate-resilient and land-use
management; (2) including gender modules during training sessions for communities and
farmer associations in the seven targeted communes on the application of community land-use
plans and implementation of climate resilient land-use practices (50 per cent of trainers will be
women); (3) establishing commune-level development councils and multi-sectoral management
structures to oversee and manage the implementation of project interventions, including
strongly encouraging women’s leadership in these institutions (with a target of 50 per cent
leadership and participation by women); and (4) drafting the provisions of Haiti’s Water Act for
the adoption and implementation of an integrated approach to water resources management in
the TR watershed, including provisions on gender responsiveness to ensure inclusive water
governance and other inclusive clauses at the policy level.

55.
The AE has identified the weak land tenure and management system as one of the risks
that could delay or prevent the implementation of the project. The feasibility study stated that

(a)
Financial sustainability beyond the project implementation period may be achieved
through the Village Saving and Credit Association (VSCA) and the budgetary
contribution from the national government. However, the VSCA under component 2 is
fully financed by co-financing, which is subject to the completion of the integrated
approach to climate-resilient flood management in component 1. The Government of
Haiti is committed to undertaking the operation and management of the project and
VSCA is expected to increase access to finance for smallholder farmers. Given the
budgetary constraints of the Haitian Government, its financial commitment is uncertain
and there is no co-financing provided by the Government. As a soft measure, it is
anticipated that the strengthened technical and institutional capacity of government
departments and communes in terms of implementing the land and water resource
management will help to enhance the sustainability of the project.
(b)
The AE carried out an economic analysis that identified an economic IRR of 41 per cent
and 43 per cent, depending on the choice of flood reduction scenarios, over 25 years.
The analysis considered the benefits from the reduction of water-borne diseases (health
benefits), reduction of infrastructure damage, and increase in the livelihood income.
With regards to the livelihood benefits, a financial analysis has been conducted at an
individual farmer’s perspective for the agroforestry activity (see paragraph 28 above).
The analysis shows that the agroforestry activity cannot be financed with loans and
farmers will have difficult in accessing additional financing such as credit. Therefore, the
full grant support is justified. As noted above, the project viability will also depend on
the capacity of the national government to take over the operation and management of
the project, and the analysis assumed that there would be no additional operation and

99.

101.
The proposed project will be implemented in Haiti, a country in which GCF is not
provided with privileges and immunities. This means that, among other things, GCF is not
protected against litigation or expropriation in this country, which risks need to be further
assessed. The GCF provided an updated draft agreement on privileges and immunities with a
bac kground note to the Government of Haiti on 25 May 2018.
102.
The Heads of the Independent Redress Mechanism and Independent Integrity Unit have
both expressed that it would not be legally feasible to undertake their redress activities and/or
investigations, as appropriate, in countries where the GCF is not provided with relevant
privileges and immunities. Therefore, it is recommended that disbursements by the GCF are
made only after the GCF has obtained satisfactory protection against litigation and
expropriation in the country, or has been provided with appropriate privileges and immunities.

Independent Technical Advisory Panel’s assessment of

I. Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel
1.
This funding proposal for a small-sized public sector adaptation project in
environmental and social safeguards category B, to be implemented over an 8-year period and
with benefits accruing over a 25-year project lifespan, is submitted by the Government of Haiti
(GoH) through the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) as accredited entity (AE),
with the Ministry of Environment of Haiti (MoE) as the executing entity (EE). The total cost of
the funding proposal (FP) is USD 31.29 million, of which USD 22.43 million is requested from
GCF, with USD 8.86 million in co-finance from Heifer International Haiti (Heifer) and UNDP.
2.
The proposed project will contribute to GCF’s paradigm shift objective of increased
climate-resilient sustainable development by enhancing the resilience of Haiti’s Trois-Rivières
(TR) watershed and its communities to the impacts of climate change intensified flooding. This
shift will be achieved by implementing a transformative approach to the way in which the GoH
and farming communities address flood impacts, incorporating ecosystem-based adaptation
(EBA), and integrated land and water resource planning and management that is informed by
climate risk. Specifically, direct investments from GCF combined with co-financing from Heifer

watershed in the country’s north-west, which is highly vulnerable to floods, that are expected to

1 .1 ICmlimpaatcet c phoantegen tbiaasli s:
4.
The FP highlights Haiti’s extreme vulnerability to climate change
impacts, as well as earthquakes (which are generally considered natural disasters). In the past
two decades, Haiti has experienced 26 floods, 12 of which wer e catastrophic, 8 hurricanes, and
numerous other tropical storms and earthquakes, with severe damage and loss caused by
climate change intensified flooding in particular. For example,in 2004, Hurricane Jeanne caused
severe flooding in the northern part of Haiti, resulting in more than 2,800 deaths and
approximately USD 41 million in damage. More recently, Hurricane Matthew struck Haiti in
20 16, causing 546 deaths and the loss of up to 90 per cent of crops and livestock in some areas.
5.
The FP and feasibility study (FS) use historical data and future projections to
demonstrate convincingly that climate change is causing an increase in annual average
temperatures and creating the conditions for increased frequency and intensity of hurricanes in
the Caribbean region. Climate change is causing a decrease in total annual rainfall in Haiti, but
also a shortening of the wet season, with a resulting increase in concentration and intensity of
rainfall events. These changing climatic conditions are contributing to an increase in the
frequency and intensity of flooding in the country, particularly in the north-western TR
w atershed of the Massif du Nord, with its steep topography.
6.
The FP also shows how climate change impacts are compounded by direct human
pressures on the environment, with degraded landscapes caused by unsustainable agricultural
practices, and historical deforestation, that involved felling of 99 per cent of the primary forest
1
cover of the country, much of this for charcoal production. During heavy rainfall events,
degraded areas experience increased surface run-off, worsened by decreased infiltration of
water into soil because of reduced vegetation cover. These factors, combined with steep slopes
and the lack of embankments along the river, increase the flow of water into the low-lying
plains, causing flooding of downstream villages. Increased water flow intensifies erosion and
causes sediment deposits in the riverbed and drainage infrastructure, further exacerbating
flooding, including in the downstream city of Port de Paix. Drinking water contaminated with
sewage and pollutants, and pools of standing floodwater increase the spread of water- and

Overall, the project will confer direct and indirect adaptation benefits to approximately

agroforestry systems and rehabilitating 7,700 ha of forests in priority areas in the TR watershed
to address the impacts of climate change-induced flooding, it is anticipated that the
interventions will reduce peak surface run-off and floodplain extents, resulting in a 35 per cent

per cent reduction in the number of households affected by 100-year flood events. This will be

and reduces flash floods; ii) reduces the soil erosion that worsens downstream flooding through

2
groundwater availability and baseflow in the dry season. Agroforestry interventions will

an d increasing agricultural production and adding value through agri-processing support.

10.
The project proponents conducted an options
analysis to choose between ‘grey’ engineered solutions to flooding, such as embankments, check
dams, canals and discharge channels on the one hand, and ‘green’ ecosystems-based solutions,
such as tree planting, natural regeneration, slope stabilization, riverbank vegetation, and
contour line farming, on the other. Green solutions were selected because they are less costly
and require less complex and expensive maintenance, and also because of the wide range of co-
be nefits they provide – for food security and human heath, ecosystem health and biodiversity.
11.
The justification for the selection of an EBA approach is set out in the FS, though it is
noted that less technical detail is provided on the green solutions in section 4 in the options
analysis. This is true also of section 7, which provides much less detail on the means of
catchment reforestation, in comparison with the technical guidance on agroforestry. In answer
to a question from the independent Technical Advisory Panel (iTAP) about how detailed
protocols would be developed for reforestation, as well as monitoring and community
engagement, the AE responded that an operations manual would be developed in year 2 of the
project, in collaboration with participating communities. The iTAP welcomes the planned
annual monitoring of dry season baseflow at four locations along the main stem of the TR river –
to provide an indicator of improvements in soil infiltration capacity as a result of upstream
reforestation. Technical monitoring protocols will be developed as part of the manual, using a
low-tech "infiltration rate tool" and “water flow metering” techniques to “increase community
engagement and limit technical dependence/maintenance without compromising accuracy of
da ta”.
12.

will be tracked, the AE highlighted the significant budget allocation (through Heifer and UNDP
co-finance) for impact analysis, evaluation and studies to monitor results – including, if/when a
flood does occur, conducting post-flood community surveys in the project intervention sites,
and integrating this with officia l data gathered by government and United Nations disaster risk

13.
In response to a query about the potential for project
impacts to be limited by the country’s fragile security situation, with lawlessness in and around
Port-au-Prince, and gangs now controlling much of Haiti’s territory, UNDP indicated that the
activities are located in relatively secure parts of Haiti, with the partial exception of Gros-Morne
and Bassin-Bleu. Nonetheless, it is acknowledged that “the security issue should be considered a
destabilizing factor that makes the operating context more prone to conflict and increases risks.
To mitigate the impact of the security situation and maximise the peacebuilding potential of the
project, a proactive approach to conflict sensitivity will be adopted and will be promoted by
3
UNDP. This will begin with a detailed conflict analysis of project sites ” as outlined in the
environmental and social management framework (section 6.1.6). A security plan and a conflict
assessment will be developed for each commune, as part of the community land-use planning
process, that “will map issues and dynamics that bring groups together and divide them,
particularly with regard to natural resources, and assess more deeply how the project may
interact with local conflict dynamics”. Procurement logistics are planned to circumvent the
capital city, and project benefits are not provided in cash, in order to reduce the risk that
be neficiaries and staff are targeted by criminal gangs in the delivery of project activities.
14.
The iTAP appreciates the conflict sensitivity analysis conducted, and the process to
continue conflict assessment and mitigation during project implementation. We note that work
on the ground in the north-west (i.e. components 1 and 2, and outputs 3.2 and 3.3), will be
supported with supplies from the region or airlifted in by the United Nations Humanitarian Air
Service, with no supplies coming by road from Port-au-Prince, which is worst affected by gang
violence and roadblocks. Having a project management office in the local directorate of the MoE
in Port-de-Paix will also mean that staff do not need to travel from the capital in the south, and
that they will help to enable effective delivery. It is noted that similar arrangements are in place
for a number of other rural projects in the MoE–UNDP environment portfolio, which currently
ha s a 90 per cent delivery rate.
15.
We remain concerned, however, about the ability of the project to carry out the national
level work of output 3.1 effectively, strengthening the national governance framework for
IWRM and scaling up the approach by establishing catchment and sub-catchment management
structures in 31 catchments across the country. This aspect, important for maximizing
adaptation impact, would appear very difficult to achieve under the current conditions, with
travel by MoE officials from the capital restricted. Even without such restrictions, it would be
challenging to establish new structures in other catchments, without the kind of in-depth
capacity development happening in the TR catchment. Under the current security situation, it
wo uld seem near impossible.
16.
Overall, the project’s adaptation impact in reducing flood risk is dependent on the
success of the reforestation and agroforestry efforts, as well as the development of the
governance framework for climate-risk informed land and water management, all of which are
taking place in a challenging socio-economic and security context. The work on the ground in
the TR watershed may have a medium to high impact potential, while the impact potential of
output 3.1 may be low, given the anticipated challenges in implementation. The iTAP assesses
the impact potential of the project as medium overall.

Overall paradigm shift
17.
: The proposed project intends to catalyse a paradigm shift in
Haiti’s approach to managing climate change intensified flooding in the TR watershed and
beyond – by initiating a shift away from the present fragmented, uncoordinated decision-
making and unsustainable land-use practices towards an integrated approach to land and water
resource management that takes into account the current and projected impacts of climate
change. Without GCF support, the GoH will continue to operate under the existing paradigm of
reactive recovery from the impacts of climate change intensified disasters, including severe
flooding, and failure to prepare for slow-onset events like drought. The project aims to
incentivize this shift and make it sustainable through an integrated approach – restoring
strategic areas of the TR catchment (C1), while promoting sustainable incomes based on
regenerative agroforestry (C2) and building a governance framework that supports rural
co mmittees to plan land use and manage catchments effectively for climate risk (C3).
18.
The lead role of MoE in executing the project, and the strong emphasis on governance
and capacity development for local government, national government and community
structures, help to embed the integrated land and water management approach to climate
change adaptation for the long term. A pathway to scaling up is built into the project through
output 3.1, although The iTAP notes the likely challenges that will be faced in carrying out inter
anlaitaional government level work, and work across all catchments nationwide, given the security
context. The intended scale-up involves amendments to Haiti’s draft Water Act to include,
, provisions for the adoption of IWRM structures across the country, and the subsequent
establishment of 31 new catchment IWRM committees, each with sub-catchment water
resource users associations. In terms of sustainability, the iTAP notes the commitment of MoE
to develop and sustain IWRM structures, and its letter to GCF, committing USD 7.5 million for
post-project operations and maintenance (O&M), supporting the “maintenance of the cost of the
gre en in

: The iTAP posed a question to the AE about whether the
intended paradigm shift might be overambitious, particularly the attempts to reforest the TR
catchment on a sustainable basis. In the context of Haiti’s extreme development challenges,
many past reforestation efforts have failed to sustain tree growth, and stakeholder structures
set up to support these efforts have often collapsed once donor funds dry up. The AE
acknowledged the depth of the challenges, but pointed to the systematic analysis conducted by
UNDP and MoE of 22 past and current related initiatives (as shown in the FS) to understand the
elements of success and failure, and to design the proposed project accordingly. Based on the
written responses and verbal interactions with the AE, the iTAP has identified three key
elements built into the project design that improve the chances of achieving the desired shift,

(a)
: Despite decades of support to agroforestry,
many farming communities maintain a focus on annual crops, because of the short-term
returns, and a lack of access to finance. In the proposed project’s output 1.2, in addition
to GCF investment in reforesting 7,700 water towers (USD 5 million), the largest single
portion of the GCF investment (USD 11 million) will go into best-practice agroforestry
support on 17,740 ha of farmers’ own land (including women-headed households).
Technical assistance will focus on maximizing the use of native and exotic tree species
with value for fruit, medicine and fodder, in combination with food crops, for which they
provide shade and soil enrichment, as well as support for beekeeping and small
livestock. The Heifer co-finance in outputs 2.1 and 2.2 will sustain this investment by
enabling commercial agroforestry as a long-term incentive for keeping trees standing –
through technical support to farmer field schools, promotion of cooperative nurseries
and agri-processing facilities, and access to appropriate micro-loans through VSCAs.
